title: Pure Structure
description: Relational possibility is represented without presupposing objects, time, geometry, or a privileged partition. This is a minimal starting point for inquiry, not an empirical claim about a pre-cosmic state.

title: Partial Separability
description: Subsystem descriptions become available relative to a factorization, scale, or access map; separability is partial, contingent, and does not establish ontological independence.

title: Domain-Relative Coherence Directions
description: Within a declared state space, geometry, constraints, and objective or profile, configurations and trajectories may be directionally compared. CU does not posit one universal scalar gradient across all domains.

title: Lawful Transitions
description: A transition relation distinguishes admissible from inadmissible changes. The law or constraint must be stated; direction cannot be inferred from relational difference alone.

title: Ordered Histories
description: Admissible transitions may support consistent precedence relations. Order can be partial and does not by itself provide metric duration or select an arrow.

title: Temporal Order and Parameterization
description: Ordered histories permit time-like parameterization when additional regularity obtains. Metric duration and a thermodynamic arrow require further assumptions.

title: Rule-Governed Transformation and Computation
description: Lawful ordered transformations may receive a computational representation once states, update rules, and representation maps are specified. Computation is not thereby established as the fundamental substance of reality.

title: Entropy and Accessibility
description: Entropy measures spread or uncertainty relative to a probability model. Coarse-graining can increase entropy while destroying accessible differentiation; entropy is not identical with inaccessible coherence.

title: Relational Geometry and Spacetime
description: Stable relational and accessibility structures may admit effective geometric representation. Lorentzian spacetime requires explicit geometric and operational bridge assumptions and is not derived from coherence alone.

title: Gravitational Dynamics
description: Einstein-type dynamics may be conditionally reconstructed under geometric, thermodynamic, and operational assumptions. The program remains incomplete and empirical.

title: Far-From-Equilibrium Organization
description: Open physical organizations can persist through throughput and dissipation. Such persistence is necessary for many living processes but is not sufficient for life.

title: Energy-Coupled Maintenance
description: Networks of internal processes harness matter and energy to maintain conditions of organization. Costs, boundaries, and contributions must be declared rather than inferred from persistence alone.

title: Active Biological Self-Maintenance
description: A candidate living organization is distinguished from passive persistence by materially realized processes whose endogenous activity helps maintain, repair, reproduce, or adaptively transform the conditions of that organization’s continuation.

title: Adaptive Problem Solving
description: Some living systems detect deviations, recruit alternatives, learn from history, and solve novel viability-relevant problems within bounded adaptive reach. This does not by itself establish consciousness.

title: Life as Coupled Autonomy
description: Life is characterized by integrated families of boundary, energy, closure, regulation, repair, heredity, viability, and evolvability capacities. No one scalar or universal threshold is assumed.

title: Representational Organization
description: Some minds and agents maintain compressed, action-relevant models of self and environment. Representation is graded and is not assumed for all life or all possible consciousness.

title: Anticipatory Regulation
description: Some systems regulate present action relative to predicted or possible futures. Predictive processing is one model family, not a universal identity of mind.

title: Learning and Error-Guided Revision
description: History-dependent mismatch can update models, policies, habits, or constraints. Correction is constrained by evidence, safety, prior organization, and the possibility of destabilization.

title: Graded Agency
description: Agency varies with action selection, counterfactual flexibility, control, learning, authorship, and stake. Agency does not imply consciousness, responsibility, or sovereignty.

title: Temporal Binding and Narrative
description: Experience and identity may integrate memory, anticipation, and present access across time. Temporal thickness is graded, history-dependent, and vulnerable to fragmentation.

title: Meaning
description: Meaning arises when states, events, relationships, and possibilities bear on real stakes, goods, histories, and trajectories. It is neither merely invented nor one fixed script.

title: Shared Representations
description: Language, symbols, records, and practices distribute meaning across agents. Shared representation enables coordination while also enabling distortion, exclusion, and narrative capture.

title: Plural Coordination
description: Social order emerges through interaction among partially autonomous agents under feedback, power, and material constraints. Coordination is not identical with consensus or legitimacy.

title: Norm Formation
description: Repeated expectations, sanctions, examples, and practices can stabilize norms. Existence, compliance, and durability do not establish justice.

title: Institutions
description: Institutions preserve rules, memory, authority, resources, and roles across time. Legitimacy requires standing, accountability, practical correctability, and bounded power.

title: Culture and Meaning Infrastructure
description: Culture transmits narratives, identities, practices, and evaluative horizons across generations. Meaning infrastructure must remain renewable, plural, truth-constrained, and open to revision.

title: Value Differentiation
description: Where beings possess welfare, agency, relationships, vulnerability, and stakes, outcomes become evaluatively distinguishable. Value is not derived from one physical scalar.

title: Harm Recognition
description: Harm concerns setbacks to welfare, agency, standing, relationship, protected conditions, or viable futures. Not every loss of organization is moral harm, and not all harm is captured by coherence language.

title: Tradeoffs Under Protected Floors
description: Conflicting goods require explicit scope, distribution, uncertainty, protected floors, noncompensation, and option-set adequacy. Aggregation alone is insufficient.

title: Justification and Public Reason
description: Norms affecting others require reasons open to evidence, affected-party testimony, independent challenge, and scrutiny for self-deception.

title: Ethical Institutions and Repair
description: Ethical systems must protect standing, agency, rights, distribution, accountability, and repair. Stability, sincerity, or procedural cleanliness alone does not make them just.

title: Engineered Sociotechnical Organization
description: Artificial systems are designed within data, labor, infrastructure, institutions, permissions, and ecological substrates. Model-level properties do not exhaust system-level coherence.

title: Objective and Option-Set Specification
description: Objectives, permissions, and presented alternatives are authored and revisable. Omitted options and hidden constraints can generate misalignment even when optimization is exact.

title: Artificial Capability and Agency
description: Artificial systems can model, plan, and act across scales, but capability, agency, perspective, responsibility, authorization, and sovereignty remain distinct.

title: Multi-Layer Alignment
description: Alignment spans behavior, process, deployment, relation, and institution. Local optimization must respect protected floors, affected parties, bounded authority, and correctability.

title: Responsibility and Governance Thresholds
description: Governance burden rises with causal reach, persistence, delegation, irreversibility, and capacity to externalize harm. Responsibility must align with authority and repair capacity.

title: Multi-Agent and Multi-Institution Alignment
description: Compatibility among powerful agents and institutions requires plural standing, conflict resolution, and independent correction rather than one imposed objective.

title: Institutional AI Governance
description: AI governance must distribute authorization, monitoring, appeal, cessation, remedy, and welfare review across sufficiently independent functions and operators.

title: Drift and Provenance Management
description: Objectives, permissions, memory, tools, feedback, models, and institutions can drift. Provenance, monitoring, versioning, and correction are continuous requirements.

title: Recursive Oversight and Correctability
description: Oversight systems must themselves be challengeable, reviewable, replaceable, and subject to remedy. No system may certify its own legitimacy solely through channels it controls.

title: Planetary Coordination
description: Planet-scale problems require coordination across jurisdictions and generations while preserving plural agency, subsidiarity, truthful records, and protected dissent.

title: Civilizational Continuity and Adaptability
description: Civilizations remain viable through material sufficiency, trustworthy information, institutional learning, ecological reciprocity, and peaceful correction—not mere persistence.

title: Existential and Irreversible Risk Governance
description: Credible severe or irreversible risks require prevention, staged exposure, containment, retained option value, and transparent necessity-and-proportionality exceptions.

title: Moral Uncertainty and Precaution
description: Ethical systems must remain responsive to uncertainty about facts, values, affected beings, and future consequences. Uncertainty neither licenses paralysis nor default deployment.

title: Plural Value Integration
description: Multiple goods and traditions can coexist under protected floors, translation, negotiated conflict, and meaningful refusal. Pluralism does not make all claims equally true or permissible.

title: Reflexive Normativity
description: Ethical principles and institutions must evaluate their own biases, power, exclusions, effects, and revision mechanisms.

title: Justificatory Integrity and Meta-Ethics
description: Systems of justification require truthful representation of facts, alternatives, affected parties, and standards. No formal model supplies its own legitimate normative content.

title: Long-Horizon Responsibility
description: Current agents and institutions bear responsibility for foreseeable effects across extended horizons, including future generations. Uncertainty and discounting must be disclosed.

title: Intergenerational Meaning
description: Meaning and obligation can extend beyond individual lifetimes through memory, inheritance, care, culture, and future-directed projects without requiring finality.

title: Collective Agency and Distributed Responsibility
description: Groups and institutions can act through structured decision processes, but responsibility remains profiled across contribution, knowledge, authority, benefit, coercion, and repair capacity.

title: Open Myth and Narrative Pluralism
canonical_role: Canonical civilizational design principle; empirical necessity hypothesis provisional
description: Civilizations may cultivate renewable narrative horizons, but shared myth must be truth-constrained, plural in thick expression, contestable in authorship, revisable, and open to refusal and exit.

title: Epistemic Humility
description: Knowledge systems must state scope, uncertainty, alternatives, and limits. Humility is active corrigibility, not equal credence for every claim.

title: Constraint Awareness and Externality Recognition
description: Systems become reflexively aware of dependencies, protected floors, externalized costs, and the conditions of their own stability.

title: Self-Limiting Power
description: Capability and authority must be bounded by standing, law, independent challenge, reversibility, and non-domination. Voluntary restraint alone is insufficient.

title: Sustainable and Correctable Optimization
description: Optimization must preserve the ecological, social, epistemic, and institutional conditions that keep goals meaningful and correction possible.

title: Universal Moral Concern
description: Moral concern widens beyond local identity to all credible loci of welfare, agency, vulnerability, relationship, and future stake, with differentiated obligations.

title: Coherence Stewardship
description: Agents and institutions undertake care for the wider material, biological, social, epistemic, and ecological conditions on which local flourishing depends.

title: Structural Wisdom
description: Patterns of successful maintenance, love, repair, and governance can be learned and transferred only with attention to context, scale, assumptions, and failure conditions.

title: Meta-Alignment and Mythic–Constitutional Governance
canonical_role: Canonical AI research and governance principle; safety efficacy unestablished
description: Alignment processes must themselves remain aligned, addressable, and corrigible. Narrative orientation may supplement but never replace constitutional floors, provenance, challenge, handoff, and exit.

title: Irreversibility Awareness
description: Actions must account for nonrecoverable loss, path dependence, lock-in, and the moral significance of retained options.

title: Existential Maturity
description: A civilization recognizes finitude, vulnerability, dependency, and the possibility of self-caused collapse, replacing innocence with proportionate responsibility.

title: Open-Ended Stability
description: Viable coherence persists through adaptation and revision without final closure, permanent equilibrium, or perfect control.

title: Meaning Without Finality
description: Objective-participatory meaning can orient finite lives and institutions without requiring one final cosmic endpoint. Commitment is compatible with open futures.

title: Coherence Universalism
canonical_role: Interpretive recognition / framework identity; commitment-register uptake
description: CU’s culminating interpretation holds that coherence under constraint is the framework’s most general organizing lens for reality and inquiry. This is an interpretive recognition and framework identity, not a theorem by exhaustive survey. In the commitment register, the recognition is taken up as a call to truthful, loving, corrigible participation in the whole.
